title: Impulse and momentum: crumple zones, airbags and coupling railway wagons
examples: How do crumple zones reduce injury?
Is kinetic energy conserved in a collision?

curves.label: Rigid car
curves.ask: Why does a rigid car feel such a big force?

curves.label: With crumple zone
curves.ask: How do crumple zones reduce injury?

explain.say: In a crash test, a 1200 kilogram car hits a wall at 15 metres per second, about 54 kilometres per hour. It must lose all its momentum, mass times velocity: 18 thousand kilogram metres per second. The question is how fast. Look at the two force spikes on the graph.

draw.text: Impulse and momentum: crumple zones, airbags and coupling railway wagons

curves.label: Rigid car
curves.ask: Why does a rigid car feel such a big force?

curves.label: With crumple zone
curves.ask: How do crumple zones reduce injury?

explain.say: Impulse is force times time, and it equals the change in momentum. On a force-time graph it is the area under the curve. The rigid car stops in 0.1 seconds, so the average force is 18 thousand divided by 0.1, which is 180 kilonewtons, with a peak near 360. See the tall narrow spike?

curves.label: Rigid car
curves.ask: Why does a rigid car feel such a big force?

curves.label: With crumple zone
curves.ask: How do crumple zones reduce injury?

explain.say: Now the car with a crumple zone stops in 0.3 seconds. Same area, same impulse, but the force is spread out: just 60 kilonewtons on average. Three times longer means a third of the force. Airbags and cricket follow-throughs work the same way. Which spike would you rather be inside?

curves.ask: Why does a rigid car feel such a big force?

curves.label: With crumple zone
curves.ask: How do crumple zones reduce injury?

explain.say: The low wide one! Now two bodies colliding. A 20 tonne railway wagon rolling at 3 metres per second hits a 10 tonne wagon at rest and they couple together. With no outside push, total momentum is conserved: 60 thousand before, so 60 thousand after. Their joint speed is 60 thousand over 30 thousand. What is it?

outputs.label: Heat and sound
outputs.ask: Is kinetic energy conserved in a collision?

explain.say: Two metres per second. But look at the energy: 90 kilojoules before, only 60 kilojoules after. The missing 30 became heat, sound and bent metal. Momentum is always conserved in a collision; kinetic energy only in a perfectly elastic one. Well done! Challenge: how fast would they move if the second wagon were also 20 tonnes?

draw.text: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy usually is not

faq.a: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts, or the area under a force-time graph. It equals the change in momentum of the body.

faq.q: Why does a rigid car feel such a big force?
faq.a: It stops in a very short time. The same change in momentum over a short time needs a very large average force.

faq.q: How do crumple zones reduce injury?
faq.a: They make the car stop over a longer time and distance. The change in momentum is the same, so a longer time means a smaller force on the people inside.
Whenever no net external force acts on the system. In a short collision, outside forces like friction are small, so the total momentum before equals the total after.

faq.q: Is kinetic energy conserved in a collision?
faq.a: Only in a perfectly elastic collision. In real collisions some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound and deformation; when bodies stick together, the loss is the largest possible.

facts: Impulse equals the change in momentum and the area under a force-time graph.
In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies move off together and the kinetic energy lost is the largest possible.

quiz.say: A 0.16 kilogram cricket ball arrives at 30 metres per second and the fielder stops it in 0.2 seconds. What is the average force?
quiz.show: 0.16 kg ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.2 s. Average force?

wrong.1: That multiplies by the time instead of dividing.
wrong.2: That is the change in momentum, not the force.

quiz.say: A 2 kilogram trolley at 4 metres per second hits a 2 kilogram trolley at rest and they stick together. What is their speed afterwards?
quiz.show: 2 kg trolley at 4 m/s sticks to a 2 kg trolley at rest. Speed after?

wrong.1: The same momentum is now shared by twice the mass, so the speed must fall.
wrong.2: That divides by four instead of sharing between the total mass of 4 kg.
